name: Dark ash
lede: Dark ash is ColorHub's name for Mizu-iro (水色), a traditional Japanese color whose name means "water color."

sections.title: Mizu-iro, the color of water
sections.body:
The Wikipedia survey "Traditional colors of Japan" lists this color under the romanized name Mizu-iro, written 水色 [1]. 水 is "water" and 色 is "color"; the library's own gloss reads "aqua blue color," and in everyday Japanese *mizu-iro* is simply the ordinary word for a pale sky-and-water blue [1]. No book consulted here independently dates the name [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[pastel-turquoise]], [[glaucous-blue]], [[grey-teal]] and [[morning-blue]], at 4.2, 4.8, 4.8 and 4.8 ΔE [1]. The hex, #86ABA5, is a modern screen approximation, not a measured dye [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within range of this swatch appears in 204 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.86 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 120 [2]. That makes it more common than 62 percent of the named colors we track [2].

It peaks in the 1900s, present in 19 of 1,674 paintings from that century, 2.4 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in just over a third of the paintings that carry it [2]. It also turns up at 4 times the expected rate within Impressionist paintings specifically [2]. The earliest dated appearance we have is Andrea del Castagno, 1450, though the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a true first sighting [2].

origin.named_after: water color, from 水 (water) and 色 (color)

openers: Dark ash's Japanese name, Mizu-iro, just means "water color" — it has nothing to do with ash.

issues: English app name (Dark ash) is a loose library match (dE 10.4) to the Japanese gloss (water color), not a translation; flagged explicitly rather than implied.
